summary: Track 15 complete: validated/corrected the 3 aquatic-roadmap parameters. Stroke cadence (0.4-1.6Hz) is well-supported. IDR struggle index (>2.5Hz) has NO traceable numeric source in the primary IDR literature — flagged as an unvalidated engineering assumption, with biomechanical bounding evidence instead. Submersion immobility timeout (>15s) is directionally reasonable but not itself literature-derived — nearest precedents (Poseidon camera systems: 10s; Kałamajska et al. 2022 wearable pulse-ox paper: ~60s max viable-detection window) bracket it.
result_text:
### Research question
Validate SPARK tracker v54's three future-work aquatic/drowning-detection parameters against published literature: (1) stroke cadence 0.4–1.6 Hz, (2) IDR struggle index >2.5 Hz vertical pressing, (3) submersion immobility timeout >15s in vertical orientation. Note gaps/corrections.

### Bottom line
Parameter 1 (stroke cadence) is **well-supported** and can be cited with confidence — it sits squarely inside the range multiple independent biomechanics/patent sources give for freestyle stroke frequency. Parameter 2 (IDR >2.5 Hz) is **not traceable to any source** — the foundational Instinctive Drowning Response literature (Pia) is purely qualitative (arm position/posture/duration, no frequency claim), and no wearable-drowning paper found quantifies struggle frequency. It should be labeled "engineering estimate, unvalidated" in the tracker rather than presented as literature-backed, though general limb-biomechanics data bounds it as plausible. Parameter 3 (>15s stillness) is **directionally reasonable but not independently validated** — it sits between the nearest real precedents (10s in deployed camera systems; a wearable paper's ~60s physiological detection window) rather than being derived from either.

### Key findings

- **Finding:** Freestyle stroke frequency reported in the literature converts to ~0.5–1.7 Hz across recreational-to-competitive swimmers, matching the tracker's 0.4–1.6 Hz band almost exactly.
  **Evidence:** A swim-analytics patent explicitly states "typical stroke rate of professional swimmers for freestyle is between 40 strokes/min and 70 strokes/min" and, for the general population, "35–95 strokes/min," recommending a 0.1–2 Hz bandpass (6–120 spm) to capture it. Independent coaching/biomechanics sources converge similarly: beginners 40–50 spm (0.67–0.83 Hz), intermediate 50–60 spm (0.83–1.0 Hz), competitive-distance 60–90 spm (1.0–1.5 Hz); elite sprint can reach 90–150 spm depending on whether "stroke" counts single-arm entries or full two-arm cycles. A peer-reviewed front-crawl accelerometer study reports the dominant cyclical (arm-stroke/body-roll) acceleration component sits "near to 1 Hz," and other swim-IMU papers use 0.5–8 Hz or 0.25–10 Hz bandpass filters to isolate the stroke-cyclical signal from noise.
  **Source:** US Patent "Methods and systems for swimming performance analysis" (image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11833392); "Analysis on the Time and Frequency Domains of the Acceleration in Front Crawl Stroke" (PMC3590863); swimswam.com, triathlete.com, theendurancestore.com, theraceclub.com (coaching secondary sources, convergent).
  **Confidence:** Established (numeric band), for the primary source; coaching sources are Supported inference / corroborating, not primary literature.
  **Relevance to SPARK:** The 0.4–1.6 Hz band is defensible as-is. Caveat worth adding to the roadmap: elite sprint freestyle, if counted as single-arm-stroke rate, can exceed 1.6 Hz (up to ~2.0–2.5 Hz) — irrelevant to SPARK's distress-detection use case (which targets struggling/fatigued swimmers, not competitive racing), but worth one sentence noting the band is scoped to non-racing conditions so a reviewer doesn't flag it as under-bounding elite performance.

- **Finding:** No source — including the foundational Instinctive Drowning Response (IDR) literature itself — specifies a frequency (Hz) for the "vertical pressing" arm movement. The >2.5 Hz figure has no traceable citation.
  **Evidence:** Pia's IDR model (as reported in the peer-reviewed "The experience of drowning," UCL, and corroborated by multiple secondary summaries) describes the behavior purely qualitatively: lateral/extended arm movements pressing down on the water, upright posture, no supporting leg kick, no voluntary control of the arms, lasting 20–60s before submersion. None of these sources — nor any of the ~10 wearable/IMU drowning-detection papers and patents surveyed (SafeSwim; the Sensors-journal "Wearable Pulse Oximeter for Swimming Pool Safety," Kałamajska et al. 2022; multiple drowning-detection patents) — report a quantified struggle/press frequency. All existing IMU-based systems found use raw acceleration-magnitude or immobility thresholds, not a frequency-domain struggle signature.
  **Source:** "The experience of drowning" (UCL, discovery.ucl.ac.uk/10139328); Wikipedia "Instinctive drowning response" (tertiary but consistent with Pia's original framing); Kałamajska, Misiurewicz & Weremczuk, "Wearable Pulse Oximeter for Swimming Pool Safety," Sensors 22(10):3823, 2022, DOI 10.3390/s22103823 (no frequency-domain struggle criterion reported).
  **Confidence:** Unresolved for the specific numeric claim (no source states it); the qualitative IDR pattern itself is Established.
  **Relevance to SPARK:** This is a genuine correction needed to the tracker. Recommend rewording from "validated" framing to "estimated" and citing IDR's qualitative pattern (upright posture + lateral/pressing arm motion + no supporting kick + 20–60s duration) as the literature-grounded part, while flagging the specific 2.5 Hz cutoff as an engineering assumption pending empirical tuning (consistent with how SPARK already treats its Layer-1 fall thresholds in §2.5 — "not empirically tuned"). Supporting bound, not validation: classic upper-limb biomechanics work (elbow-oscillation power-spectral studies) puts the maximum frequency of voluntary rhythmic arm movement at ~4–6 Hz for the elbow alone (open-loop/preprogrammed above ~2 Hz), with whole-arm/shoulder movements (larger inertia, as in an IDR press) expected lower than isolated-elbow figures — so 2.5 Hz is biomechanically plausible as an upper-range panic-driven whole-arm rate, but this is an indirect bound from non-drowning biomechanics literature, not a drowning-specific validation.

- **Finding:** ">15s stillness in vertical orientation" as a submersion-immobility timeout is the same order of magnitude as, but not directly derived from, the nearest real precedents.
  **Evidence:** The most-deployed commercial analogy — Poseidon computer-vision pool systems (240+ installations) — triggers an alarm at exactly 10s of detected stillness at the pool bottom; SwimEye reports similar (~10s) figures. On the wearable-sensor side, the only closely comparable peer-reviewed device (Kałamajska et al. 2022, Sensors) uses accelerometer-detected non-movement as a gate to activate an SpO2/heart-rate check, within a modeled drowning-phase framework where the pre-irreversible "stationary" phase lasts "up to a maximum of 60 s" — i.e., their algorithm's usable detection window is up to 60s, not a 15s hard alarm. Separately, a 2020-era drowning-safety-device patent (US20220309897A1) uses exactly this architecture — accelerometer for orientation/depth + a submersion timer that alarms after a settable time value — directly precedenting "orientation + elapsed-stillness timer" as a design pattern, without fixing 15s specifically. Popular-science claims that cerebral hypoxia causes unconsciousness "within approximately 15 seconds" exist but are non-peer-reviewed and inconsistent with other secondary sources citing 30–90s+ for voluntary breath-hold before involuntary gasping.
  **Source:** poseidon-tech.com / drowningprevention.com.au (commercial technical documentation, consistent across multiple independent write-ups); Kałamajska et al., Sensors 2022, DOI 10.3390/s22103823; US20220309897A1 "Wearable Safety Device for Swimming" (Google Patents); "System, device, and method of detecting dangerous situations," US Patent 10803724 (explicitly proposes accelerometer/gyroscope/compass-based "unusually vertical for long periods... or at least not moving in orientation" as a drowning cue — direct precedent for combining orientation + stillness, exactly SPARK's proposed criterion).
  **Confidence:** Supported inference (the timeout concept and orientation+stillness combination are well-precedented; the specific 15s value is not independently derived from any single source — it sits between 10s [camera, faster/more false-positive-prone] and 60s [wearable-paper's outer bound]).
  **Relevance to SPARK:** 15s is a reasonable, defensible middle ground — closer to the fast/aggressive camera-system value than to the wearable paper's 60s ceiling — and is architecturally validated by at least one patent using the identical orientation+timer combination via wrist/neck-worn accelerometer. Recommend citing the Poseidon precedent and the US20220309897A1 patent as grounding for the *architecture* (orientation-gated stillness timer), while being explicit in the thesis that 15s itself is SPARK's own choice, not a literature-derived number, pending empirical tuning — same honesty framing recommended for Parameter 2.

- **Finding (secondary, worth folding into the roadmap):** Wrist placement (SPARK's locked enclosure location, §2.2) is measurably less accurate for stroke-cyclical recognition than back/sacrum placement in the literature.
  **Evidence:** A systematic review of inertial sensor swimming-analysis studies reports a back-worn sensor achieved 95.3% stroke-identification accuracy at 25 Hz vs. 89.8% for a wrist-worn sensor at the same rate (Siirtola et al., cited within).
  **Source:** "Inertial Sensor Technology for Elite Swimming Performance Analysis: A Systematic Review," PMC4732051.
  **Confidence:** Established (reported experimental comparison).
  **Relevance to SPARK:** Not a blocker (this is future-work scope, not a build task), but worth one sentence in the roadmap noting that SPARK's existing wrist-worn hardware form factor (locked for the fall-detection use case) will likely see modestly reduced stroke/IDR-pattern recognition accuracy versus a trunk-worn placement, if this extension is ever implemented on the same hardware.

### Evidence table

| Finding | Evidence | Source | Confidence | SPARK implication |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stroke cadence 0.4–1.6 Hz | Multiple independent sources converge on ~0.5–1.7 Hz for freestyle stroke rate | US Patent 11833392; PMC3590863; coaching secondary sources | Established | Keep as-is; add one-line scope caveat re: elite sprint edge case |
| IDR struggle >2.5 Hz | No source states any struggle frequency; IDR literature is qualitative only | UCL "Experience of drowning"; Wikipedia; Kałamajska et al. 2022 (Sensors) | Unresolved (numeric); Established (qualitative pattern) | Reword as engineering estimate, not literature-validated; cite qualitative IDR pattern instead |
| Submersion timeout >15s | 10s (camera systems, deployed) and ~60s (wearable paper's window) bracket it; no direct 15s source | poseidon-tech.com; Kałamajska et al. 2022; US20220309897A1; US10803724 | Supported inference | Keep 15s as reasonable middle value; cite architecture precedent, flag exact value as SPARK's own choice |
| Wrist placement less accurate than trunk for stroke recognition | 95.3% (back) vs 89.8% (wrist) at 25Hz | PMC4732051 (systematic review) | Established | Add as a roadmap caveat re: existing hardware form factor |

### Contradictions and limitations

- No wearable-IMU-specific, peer-reviewed source was found that validates a frequency-domain "struggle index" for drowning at all — this is a genuine literature gap, not just a SPARK-specific gap, so Parameter 2 cannot be fully resolved by more searching within this track's scope; it would need either (a) rewording to avoid implying validation, or (b) primary empirical data SPARK itself would have to collect.
- Secondary/popular-science sources on time-to-unconsciousness during drowning (15s, 30–45s, 1–2min, "few minutes") are mutually inconsistent and mostly non-peer-reviewed blog content; none were treated as load-bearing evidence for Parameter 3 above — the peer-reviewed Kałamajska et al. figure (≤60s usable window) and the commercial Poseidon figure (10s) were used instead as the credible anchors.
- Stroke-rate literature has a counting-convention ambiguity (single-arm strokes/min vs. full two-arm cycles/min) that roughly doubles reported numbers depending on source; this was reconciled by preferring the patent's explicit Hz/bandpass framing over strokes-per-minute folklore, but it's worth SPARK stating its own counting convention explicitly when this roadmap item is eventually specified further.
- Sample coverage: no primary-source paper specific to Nepal-context or non-competitive/panicked-swimmer populations was found for any of the three parameters (all found sources are competitive-swimming biomechanics, commercial pool-safety systems, or general drowning-physiology literature) — consistent with this being future-work scope rather than a validated build-ready spec.

### Recommendation

Update the v54 roadmap text to: (1) keep the 0.4–1.6 Hz stroke-cadence band, optionally citing the swim-analytics patent's 0.1–2 Hz general bandpass recommendation and noting the band targets non-racing/distress conditions; (2) relabel the IDR struggle-index parameter as an engineering estimate pending empirical tuning rather than implying it is literature-derived, and cite the qualitative Pia/IDR pattern (upright posture, lateral/pressing arm motion, no supporting kick, 20–60s duration) as what the literature actually supports; (3) keep 15s for the submersion-immobility timeout but cite it as SPARK's own choice bracketed by the 10s (camera-system) / ~60s (wearable-paper) precedents, and cite US10803724 / US20220309897A1 as architectural precedent for the orientation+timer combination; (4) add a one-sentence note that wrist placement (SPARK's locked hardware form factor) is empirically less accurate than trunk placement for stroke-pattern recognition, should this roadmap item ever move from future-work to implementation.
